clue.text: Theatre seats on the house all round? Not half!

definitions.text: Theatre seats on the house all round? Not half!

parts.words: Theatre seats on the house all round? Not half!
parts.note: a tier of theatre seats running all the way round the auditorium is a circle; take only half of that ring and you have the shape described

explanation.surface: A theatre is giving away seats all round the house, and someone answers with the emphatic slang 'Not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' reads as British slang for 'absolutely!', and 'on the house' as 'free'; really the dress circle runs round the house, and only half of that ring is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring of seats curving halfway round a stage is a half-round shape, the classic layout of an amphitheatre.

clue.text: Kneeler has this covering

indicators.note: the clue says a kneeler is 'has' plus this, so this stands for whatever is left once those three letters are taken off

parts.note: a hassock is a cushion to kneel on in church
taken as written

explanation.surface: A churchgoer's kneeler comes with its own protective cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a sum: HASSOCK, a church kneeler, is HAS followed by 'this', so 'this' is the rest of the word, which is also a foot covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A sock is a knitted garment that covers the foot.

clue.text: Child makes small contribution

definitions.meaning: a tiny youngster, as in 'poor little thing'
the widow's offering in the Gospel story, two small coins given from her poverty

explanation.definitionFit: A mite is both a small child and a tiny gift, from the biblical widow who gave two coins.

clue.text: Term one clearly described to do with style of writing

definitions.text: to do with style of writing

parts.note: to term something is to call it that name
I is the Roman numeral for one
a graphic account is vivid and clearly described

explanation.surface: A teacher clearly explains a term relating to the style of someone's writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Calligraphy is the art of fine handwriting, so the adjective concerns penmanship and the look of written letters.

clue.text: Lost one's temper with the Royal and Ancient

parts.note: very old, as in aged

explanation.surface: Someone flew into a fury at the Royal and Ancient, the St Andrews golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Royal and Ancient' looks like one name, the governing golf club at St Andrews in Scotland, but split it: R for Royal and AGED for Ancient, with 'and' just joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: To rage is to be furiously angry, so having raged is having flown into a fury.

clue.text: Laid-back, certainly, under a garland of flowers

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits beneath the first, so the word for certainly goes under the garland

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers
surely means certainly

explanation.surface: Someone relaxed, certainly, lounging beneath a garland of flowers on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Unhurried and relaxed, a leisurely manner is easy-going and calm.

clue.text: Officer promoted after this?

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for a commanding officer
raised in rank, moved up

explanation.surface: An officer finds himself promoted after a sudden seizure of power.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: after an army overthrows a government, its officers tend to be promoted.
explanation.definitionFit: A military takeover of a government often rewards the plotting officers with rank, as the clue's question hints.

clue.text: Cause apoplexy — nothing ever goes wrong with Times quote

parts.note: O looks like a zero, nothing

indicators.note: the word ever going wrong means its letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as times
to cite is to quote

explanation.surface: Nothing ever goes wrong with the Times newspaper's quotations, a claim to drive a reader to apoplexy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes wrong' rearranges EVER to VERE. 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexcite someone is to agitate them so much they could have a fit of rage.

clue.text: Man who noted the lightest rain falling

parts.note: palest means lightest in colour

indicators.note: rain falling is rain coming down in a tumble, so its letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A man notes down that the lightest rain is falling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling' turns RAIN into RINA. 'Man who noted' means a man who wrote notes: Giovanni Palestrina, the Italian Renaissance composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Palestrina was a sixteenth-century Italian composer of church music, a man who set down musical notes.

clue.text: Neat diagram showing territorial boundary of Jersey, perhaps

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle
a grid is a diagram of squares or lines

explanation.surface: A tidy map shows the territorial boundary of the Channel Island of Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like 'tidy' but is the old word for cattle, and Jersey is a breed of cow rather than the Channel Island.
explanation.definitionFit: A cattle grid is a set of bars over a ditch at a road that cows will not cross, so it fences in a herd's ground.

clue.text: The old brief will is to be found in the Shetlands

definitions.text: to be found in the Shetlands

parts.note: ye is an archaic form of the
'll is the shortened form of will, as in I'll

explanation.surface: An old will, brief as it was, turned up in the Shetland Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will' looks like a legal document; it is the verb, shortened to 'll. Yell is one of the Shetland Islands, off the north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Yell is the second largest island of the Shetland group, so it is located among those islands.

clue.text: Gérolstein's ruler is a dignified costermonger's wife

parts.note: grand means stately and dignified
in Cockney slang a man calls his wife his duchess, or 'my old dutch'

explanation.surface: The ruler of Gérolstein turns out to be a dignified street trader's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Offenbach's operetta 'La Grande-Duchesse de Gérolstein' supplies the ruler. A costermonger is a London street seller of fruit, and Cockneys call a wife 'duchess'. The paper prints the length as (7), a misprint for 12.
explanation.definitionFit: Offenbach's comic opera is about the Grand Duchess who rules the imaginary state of Gérolstein.

clue.text: Rear deer here?

definitions.meaning: the back end of an animal, its rump
a female deer is a hind, and the lodgings she lives in would be her living quarters

explanation.definitionFit: The back parts of a four-legged animal are its rump; split in two the word is a female deer's lodgings.

clue.text: Part of the race properly left to the gods

parts.note: a long race like a cycle tour is run in stages
rightly, in the right way

explanation.surface: Part of a race, properly speaking, is left in the hands of the gods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the gods' are the highest gallery seats in a theatre. Stage directions are given from the actor's view, so the actor's right is the left side as seen by the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage directions face the audience, so the actor's right side appears on the left to spectators up in the gallery.

clue.text: Railway worker — in the dining car?

definitions.meaning: a man who lays and maintains the rails and sleepers of a track
a waiter setting out dishes on the tables of a train's restaurant carriage would be laying plates

explanation.definitionFit: A platelayer is a track maintenance worker; whimsically, someone setting dishes on dining tables.

clue.text: Fairly decent beer — all to get drunk

indicators.note: the letters getting drunk stagger about into a new order

explanation.surface: A fairly decent beer, enough for everyone to get drunk on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get drunk' scrambles BEER, ALL and TO together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something passable or acceptable is bearable enough to put up with, middling rather than good.

clue.text: Meeting admits a guest free as a graceful act

indicators.note: a meeting admitting someone takes them inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a bee is a gathering of people, as in a sewing bee

indicators.note: the letters of a guest are set free to move into another order

explanation.surface: A gathering lets in a guest without charge, as a gracious gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' suggests an encounter, but here it is a bee, a gathering as in a spelling bee; 'free' is the anagram signal, not 'without charge'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beau geste is French for a fine gesture, a magnanimous act done for show or generosity.

clue.text: Better name the person finishing the cake

parts.note: an icer puts the icing on a cake as the final touch

explanation.surface: Better to name whoever puts the finishing touches to the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicer is the comparative of nice, more pleasant and so an improvement.

clue.text: Study to become stronger

definitions.meaning: to work at a subject in order to learn it
of wind, to rise and blow harder

explanation.definitionFit: One learns a subject thoroughly by getting it up, and a wind gets up when it strengthens.

clue.text: Not working with 'and'? Yes!

indicators.note: letters working are set in motion and moved around into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a thing is broken when the word 'and' is used, and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges NOT, AND and YES. The whole clue also defines: the figure of speech that works without 'and', leaving conjunctions out.
explanation.definitionFit: Asyndeton is the rhetorical figure that omits conjunctions, as in 'I came, I saw, I conquered'.

clue.text: Loaded cattle-trucks

parts.note: rolling in it means rich, loaded with money
livestock, farm animals

explanation.surface: Cattle-trucks loaded and ready to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cattle-trucks' reads as one compound, but split at the hyphen: 'cattle' is wordplay and 'trucks' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolling stock is the railway's wagons, carriages and locomotives that run on the track.

clue.text: Watch is untrustworthy after two

definitions.meaning: a timepiece or a device for measuring time
add this word after 'two' and you get a cheat who deceives a partner

explanation.definitionFit: A timer measures time like a stopwatch, and a two-timer is an unfaithful lover.

clue.text: Soprano needs help with high note

parts.note: aid means help
A is a musical note

explanation.surface: A soprano needs assistance to reach a high note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soprano' is a role, not a singer: Aida is the soprano lead in Verdi's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's heroine, the Ethiopian princess, is sung by a soprano, so she stands for one.

clue.text: Old advice for producing musical pipe sound

indicators.note: the clue asks for the pronunciation of the word for a musical pipe, not its spelling

parts.note: a reed is a pipe of cane, or the vibrating strip in a wind instrument

explanation.surface: Old advice on how to produce a sound from a musical pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Rede is an archaic word for counsel, as in Shakespeare's 'recks not his own rede'.

clue.text: Portraitist was a gentile originally

parts.note: goy is a Yiddish word for a non-Jew

explanation.surface: A portrait painter is said to have been born a gentile.
explanation.walkthrough: Goya, the Spanish painter, was a court portraitist. The clue's 'a gentile' gives A and GOY, which are written the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco Goya was the Spanish court painter famous for royal portraits.

clue.text: Hot meal is cooked, I note, for leper

indicators.note: cooked suggests ingredients mixed and transformed, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A hot meal is cooked, I note, for someone with leprosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges H, MEAL and IS into ISHMAEL. 'leper' is used figuratively for a social outcast, as Ishmael was cast out in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ishmaelite is a social outcast, after Abraham's son Ishmael, sent into the wilderness; a leper is figuratively one shunned by all.

clue.text: Half-time

definitions.meaning: at some English public schools, such as Eton, a school session is called a half
a fixed period, as in a prison sentence or a period of office

explanation.definitionFit: A school session is called a half at Eton, and a fixed period of duration is a stretch.

clue.text: Peace of mind found in bed

definitions.meaning: a flower grown in a garden flower bed, the wild pansy

explanation.definitionFit: Heartsease means tranquillity, and it is also the wild pansy, a garden flower.
